message.reasoning:
I need to make a Monopoly decision.

Only p4 remains. I have $535 and am on STATES_AVENUE. My dark blues are fully built with hotels. The opponent has browns, railroads, and utilities.

I am mapping the opponent's properties to standard Monopoly sets. He owns browns, light blues, pinks, and yellows.

The opponent's browns, light blues, and yellows are all incomplete monopolies. Boardwalk and Park Place hotels would cost him $2000 and $1500 in rent. He has only $363 cash plus building equity to liquidate.

Each brown hotel sells for $125, so both are worth $250. Combined with his $363 cash, p4 can liquidate roughly $613 total. That is far below the $2000 rent on Boardwalk and $1500 on Park Place.

The opponent must sell his brown hotels before mortgaging any property, since buildings block mortgage. After selling the two hotels for $250, he can mortgage the remaining unmortgaged properties for roughly $980. Combined with his $363 cash, his liquidation capacity drops to about $1593.

Boardwalk is the kill. Park Place is survivable but leaves the opponent nearly broke. I will end my turn.

I am weighing whether to build on Kentucky. It is the only buildable property, and adding one house would cost $150. That would even out my red set and raise rent to about $250. The opponent is currently on VENTNOR_AVENUE.

Building on Kentucky would cost $150 and leave me with only $385. That is below the $450 rent on Baltic hotel, so I might need to sell a house to pay it. I will wait for my next roll instead.

I am now considering unmortgaging my orange set. It would cost $308 to bring back St. James, Tennessee, and New York. After that I would have about $227 left to build two houses there. I am checking whether the resulting rent is worth the cash outlay.

Unmortgaging the orange set would not create a stronger kill than Boardwalk. I must keep my cash cushion so I can pay rent without selling the Boardwalk hotel. If I sell it to pay rent, the opponent could survive with four houses at $1400 instead of $2000. I need to avoid selling buildings entirely.

I am calculating the opponent's remaining rent threats. Baltic hotel is $450, Mediterranean hotel is $250, and both utilities cap at $120. The railroads pay $50. Marvin Gardens, Pacific, and North Carolina are all unimproved with no monopolies, so their base rent is low.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

I am player 2 with $535 and no jail. The other players are bankrupt. I own all three orange properties but they are mortgaged. I also own the pink and light blue properties, though those are incomplete sets.

I own a red monopoly with two houses on Indiana and Illinois. My dark blue set is complete with hotels on both properties. The yellow properties are mortgaged and incomplete. I also hold the B&O and Short Line railroads.

The opponent has $363, a Get Out of Jail Free card, and a brown hotel monopoly. They are currently in jail.

The opponent's green properties are incomplete. They need my Pennsylvania to complete the set.

I am calculating whether I can force a bankruptcy by selling my dark blue hotels. Boardwalk and Park Place each rent $2000 and $1500. The opponent has only $363 cash. Brown hotels sell back for half their purchase price.

Selling both brown hotels returns $250. Unmortgaged properties can be mortgaged for their face value to raise cash. I am now calculating the opponent's full liquidation.

The opponent's liquidation totals roughly $1,593. Their unmortgaged properties are worth about $980 in mortgage cash. Selling the two brown hotels returns $250. Combined with their $363 cash, this exceeds the $1,000 needed to force bankruptcy.

Boardwalk's $2000 rent exceeds the opponent's liquidation of $1,593, so a landing there would bankrupt them. Park Place's $1,500 rent is below that threshold, so they could survive there.

The opponent is in jail and may stay there to avoid the board.

I am on New York Avenue with $535 cash. A Baltic hotel hit of $450 is manageable.

I will not build on Kentucky. I will not unmortgage properties. I will not trade away Pennsylvania or cash.

The opponent is in jail with a Get Out of Jail Free card. They can pay $50, use the card, or roll doubles to leave. I need them to land on Boardwalk to force bankruptcy. If they stay in jail for three turns, they must eventually move.

The opponent wants to stay in jail to avoid my hotels. I will not give them reasons to leave and will keep my cash cushion intact. I am now weighing the available actions for this turn.

Building a house on Kentucky would cost $150 and leave me with only $385. That is $65 short of surviving a Baltic hotel hit, so I must avoid building entirely.

I am now considering whether a trade could entice the opponent to leave jail and land on Boardwalk.

I am now considering selling the Boardwalk hotel to raise cash. That would remove the $2,000 kill shot, but four houses on Boardwalk still yield $1,700 in rent. I am recalculating whether that is enough to force bankruptcy given the opponent's current liquidation.

Four houses on Boardwalk yield $1,700 in rent, which exceeds the opponent's liquidation of $1,593. This confirms that even without a hotel, landing there would bankrupt them. The hotel is merely extra insurance.

Selling the Boardwalk hotel would return $500 and leave me with $1,035 cash. Four houses there would still yield $1,700 in rent, which exceeds the opponent's liquidation of $1,593. The extra margin is only about $107, so selling the hotel is not worth it. Keeping the hotel is safer because the $407 gap to bankruptcy is more comfortable than a tighter margin. I will not trade away the opponent's Get Out of Jail Free card.

The opponent cannot complete any property set. They lack the pink and light blue monopolies, and they need my Pennsylvania to finish the green set. I hold all orange, red, and dark blue properties.

I am on New York Avenue and must decide whether to end my turn or take another action.

I have already resolved the turn's mandatory actions. I am on New York Avenue, which is mortgaged, so no rent is due. I will end my turn without spending or trading away any properties.

Green hotels would yield $1,400 on Pennsylvania, $1,275 on North Carolina, and $1,275 on Pacific. Even three houses on greens would be lethal. The opponent cannot afford to unmortgage Pennsylvania or build houses with only $363 cash. I will not trade away that property.

Unmortgaging all three orange properties would cost $308. That leaves only $227, which is too little to build even one house on each property. The doubled rent from an unmortgaged orange monopoly is negligible at roughly $28 to $32 per turn. This makes unmortgaging the set unprofitable.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.

Combined with cash and building sales, player four's liquidation assets reach one thousand six hundred eighty-three dollars. Boardwalk is the only lethal square, since its rent of two thousand dollars exceeds that total by three hundred seventeen dollars. Park Place would leave them with one hundred eighty-three dollars, so it is not fatal. I am now cataloguing my survival risks.

I will sell all five red houses to raise cash to eight hundred twenty dollars. I will keep both hotels so they remain my win condition.

Player four is deliberately hiding in jail with a Get Out of Jail Free card to avoid Boardwalk. I am now checking whether I can increase the Boardwalk rent.

A trade for their high-value properties would likely be rejected as bad deals. I realized that selling all red houses would backfire. Player four's rent on Illinois Avenue would drop from three hundred dollars to forty, which would shrink the cash gap toward Boardwalk rather than widen it. Keeping those houses is actually the safer defensive move.

Keeping two houses on Illinois Avenue is the safer defensive move. Player four's cash gap to survive Boardwalk drops from three hundred seventeen dollars to one hundred seventeen dollars if they pass GO once. A single rent payment of three hundred dollars would restore that shortfall. Selling all red houses would remove that drain and shrink the kill margin instead of widening it.

I will sell one house from Indiana Avenue. That keeps the even-build rule and leaves two houses on Illinois Avenue. Cash becomes five hundred twenty dollars. Baltic Avenue rent is four hundred fifty dollars, leaving seventy dollars. Street repairs cost three hundred ninety dollars, leaving one hundred thirty dollars. This is tight but survivable.

I cannot sell two red houses at once. Removing one Indiana house while keeping Illinois at two would break the even-build rule. I must keep one house on Indiana and leave Illinois at two.
